title: Brazil is defining what a deepfake is, five weeks before it votes
content:
Brazil votes on October 4, and its electoral court spent Tuesday working through a question that many regulators are still struggling to answer: what exactly counts as a deepfake?
The Tribunal Superior Eleitoral was expected to rule on broader restrictions for AI-generated campaign material, Reuters reported.
The proposed rules go beyond simply banning deceptive deepfakes. They would require AI-generated campaign material to be labelled, prohibit systems that recommend candidates, and introduce a blackout period during which new synthetic political content could not be published or promoted immediately before and after voting.
The definition matters because Brazil has already encountered a case that sits awkwardly between disclosure and deception.
In July, Jair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest and barred from public communication, appeared at his son’s campaign launch as an AI-generated avatar that explicitly identified itself as a simulation.
That disclosure is central to the legal argument. Brazil’s existing electoral rules target fabricated content that can mislead voters, but an AI avatar that openly tells viewers it is an AI representation does not fit neatly into that definition.
Lula’s coalition petitioned the TSE, arguing that the video still violated rules governing synthetic content used to influence voters.
Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign responded that a clearly labelled simulation should not be treated as a deepfake, an argument that is difficult to dismiss if the definition is based primarily on whether viewers are being deceived.
The court itself has shown some disagreement over where that line should sit. TSE president Kássio Nunes Marques has suggested that AI-generated campaign material can be permissible when it does not cause harm, while Supreme Court justice Alexandre de Moraes has warned that the same technology could violate Bolsonaro’s house-arrest restrictions and contribute to electoral disinformation.
Brazil already had rules covering AI before this election. The TSE introduced requirements ahead of the 2024 municipal elections, including disclosure of synthetic content, which helps explain why the Bolsonaro avatar was presented as a simulation rather than as an attempt to impersonate him without disclosure.
Tuesday’s ruling is expected to provide a clearer definition of what is and is not permitted, although the timing is difficult.
With five weeks remaining before a national election, campaigns, platforms and regulators will have very little time to adjust to whatever framework the court establishes.
The problem Brazil is trying to address exists far beyond its borders. Disclosure-based rules, including those being developed under the EU’s AI Act, are built around the assumption that telling people when content has been generated or manipulated by AI can reduce its ability to mislead them.
The Bolsonaro case puts that assumption under pressure because the content can be completely transparent about its synthetic nature and still be politically persuasive.
There is also a question that the existing rules were not really designed to answer. A politician who is legally prohibited from speaking publicly but appears through an AI-generated representation has not physically addressed the crowd, yet the political message can reach voters almost as effectively as if the politician had been standing there in person.
The proposed restrictions on recommendation systems introduce a separate problem because they move beyond the content itself and into the way platforms distribute political material.
Prohibiting algorithms from recommending particular candidates would require regulators to examine ordinary platform mechanics, which is considerably more difficult to monitor than whether an individual video carries an AI disclosure.
Brazil has more experience with this kind of intervention than many countries. Its courts have been willing to take a more active role in regulating online platforms and political speech, and the TSE had already established AI-specific electoral rules before the current campaign began.
Enforcement is likely to be more difficult than defining the rules. A blackout on synthetic political content around election day is useful only if someone can identify synthetic material quickly enough to stop it from spreading, which becomes particularly difficult when content moves through private messaging groups rather than public social networks.
The blackout provision is also the least tested part of the proposal. Treating AI-generated political content as a separate category that requires a quiet period around an election is a significant step beyond existing European rules, which generally focus on transparency and the circumstances in which synthetic content can be misleading.
European regulators therefore have a practical reason to watch what happens in Brazil.
The EU’s own transparency requirements rely on some of the same assumptions about disclosure, while European elections have yet to produce a comparable case involving a politician who is prohibited from communicating but can still reach voters through an AI-generated representation.
The scale of Brazil’s electorate makes enforcement harder still. More than 150 million people are eligible to vote, and messaging apps are deeply embedded in political communication, much of it taking place in private conversations and groups that regulators cannot realistically monitor in the same way as public posts.
Brazil is therefore trying to establish the boundaries while the campaign is already under way, and the political actors affected by those boundaries have a direct interest in how they are drawn.
Leaving the rules undefined would create its own problems, but establishing them only weeks before voters go to the polls leaves very little room for regulators, campaigns and platforms to learn how they work.
The election takes place on October 4, leaving the TSE with roughly five weeks for whatever rules it approved on Tuesday to be tested in practice.

report.summary: 巴西选举法院在投票前五周明确何为深度伪造，拟推严格新规。
report.background: 巴西10月4日举行全国选举，最高选举法院(TSE)正忙于定义深度伪造。此前，被软禁且禁止公开沟通的博尔索纳罗以明确标识为AI生成的头像出现在儿子竞选活动中，引发争议。巴西已有针对AI竞选内容的披露规则，但缺乏清晰定义。此次裁决拟要求AI材料标注、禁止算法推荐候选人，并设置投票前后合成内容黑名单期。此举不仅影响巴西，也牵动全球监管神经，欧洲监管者正密切关注。
key_points: 巴西TSE拟推新规，要求AI生成的竞选材料必须明确标注，禁止平台算法推荐特定候选人，并在投票前后设有合成政治内容发布黑名单期。
博尔索纳罗AI头像案成定义难点：虽明确标明为模拟，仍被指控影响选民，法院内部对此意见不一。
新规执行面临挑战：私人消息群组难以监控，快速识别合成内容难度大，黑名单期缺乏既有实践。
巴西案例打破“披露即可防误导”假设，给欧盟AI法案等披露机制带来压力，监管者正密切关注。
report.impact: 对AI行业，监管清晰化将增加生成式AI在政治传播中的合规成本，促使企业内置内容来源认证。对开发者，需研发更可靠的深伪检测与标注工具，并注意推荐算法合规。对普通用户，AI内容透明度提升有助于识别操纵，但过度限制可能影响表达，且私人传播漏洞仍存。全球监管规则将因巴西实践而加速演化。
report.tools: 可关注开源深伪检测工具（如Deepware Scanner、FakeCatcher）和内容来源认证标准（C2PA），以便跟进AI内容标注。同时追踪巴西TSE官方裁决及欧盟AI法案实施细则，了解合规要求。
